strengths: The paper addresses a clear gap: existing VR sketch-to-shape methods discard stroke/point ordering and treat sketches as unordered point clouds. The proposed order-aware encoding is a well-motivated, technically sound design choice.

Introduces a new open, multi-category (4 categories) dataset with 20k synthetic and 900 real sketch-shape pairs, which is substantially larger and more diverse than the only prior public benchmark (3DVRChair, single-category, 1005 pairs). This is a useful community resource.

The synthetic sketch generation pipeline (surface sampling -> saliency sub-sampling -> spline fitting -> culling -> stroke ordering) is fully automatic/training-free and reduces reliance on costly human annotation, while a surface-snapping VR interface improves real-data quality (supported by lower asymmetric Chamfer distance vs. other real datasets in Table 1).

Comprehensive experiments: comparisons against two baselines (LAS-Diffusion, Luo et al.) on both 3DVRChair and the new dataset, few-shot adaptation study, cross-modal/partial-sketch completion experiment, and a thorough ablation study (ordering, augmentation, pretraining, alternate encoder, alternate sketch formats) that convincingly isolates the contribution of order-awareness (F-score drops from 56.8 to 48.9 without ordering).

Results show large, consistent improvements over baselines (e.g., >60% CD reduction and >40% F-score improvement on 3DVRChair), and the partial-sketch completion results are a practically relevant capability for iterative VR design workflows.
Reasonable implementation and reproducibility details (architecture dimensions, training schedule, inference speed, hardware) are reported, and code/data release is promised.
weaknesses: The real evaluation set is small (400 pairs, 100 per category) and the real training/fine-tuning data is also limited (900 total real sketches collected from only 15 participants), which raises concerns about statistical robustness and generalization of the reported gains, especially given the significant effort (225 person-hours) required to scale further.

The chosen F-score threshold (delta=0.02) is stated to be selected specifically to accommodate manual sketching imprecision, but no sensitivity analysis across thresholds is shown, making it hard to judge robustness of the reported margins.

The reliance on a frozen pretrained 3D VQ-VAE (from SDFusion) with 64^3 SDF resolution is explicitly acknowledged as a bottleneck limiting fine geometric detail; this ceiling is inherited rather than addressed, and the paper does not explore whether end-to-end or higher-resolution training would change relative rankings.

The synthetic sketch generation heuristic (Bezier spline fitting, saliency thresholds, culling thresholds, DFS stroke ordering with 10% stochastic skipping) has many hand-tuned hyperparameters whose sensitivity/generality across object categories beyond the four studied (chair, table, cabinet, airplane) is not analyzed.

Comparison baselines are somewhat limited — Chen et al. is excluded due to lack of released code/checkpoints, and LAS-Diffusion is adapted from a 2D-image setting, which may not be a fully optimized comparison; a more recent 3D VR-sketch method (VRSketch2Gaussian, listed as concurrent/2025 in references) is not compared.

The ordered stroke assumption depends on synthetic heuristics (DFS traversal with random skipping) to approximate human drawing order for training data; it's unclear how well this heuristic order matches actual human stroke sequences, potentially limiting the fidelity of the order signal learned from synthetic data despite the paper's claims of successful synthetic-to-real transfer.
The paper does not report variance or statistical significance (e.g., across multiple runs or seeds) for the main quantitative comparisons, given the modest evaluation set sizes.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated task formulation: treating VR sketches as temporally ordered stroke/point sequences rather than unordered point clouds, explicitly modeling drawing order which prior VR-sketch-to-shape works discard.

Contributes an open, multi-category dataset (VRSKETCH2SHAPE) with over 20k synthetic and 900 real hand-drawn sketch-shape pairs across 4 categories, substantially larger and more diverse than the only prior public benchmark (3DVRChair, single category, 1005 pairs).

Proposes a fully automatic, training-free heuristic pipeline (surface sampling, saliency sub-sampling, spline fitting, culling, stroke ordering) for generating realistic sequential synthetic sketches at scale, avoiding costly human annotation.
The order-aware BERT-style sketch encoder coupled with SDFusion diffusion generator is a sensible, clearly described architecture, and the paper reports clear end-to-end single-stage training.
Strong empirical results: outperforms prior sketch-to-shape baselines (Luo et al., LAS-Diffusion) by large margins on both the existing 3DVRChair benchmark and the new dataset in CD and F-score.

Thorough ablation study isolates the contribution of stroke ordering, augmentation strategies, pretraining, and sequential vs. alternative sketch representations (point clouds, multiview images), convincingly supporting the paper's central claim that 'order matters'.

Demonstrates practically useful capabilities beyond the main task, including few-shot synthetic-to-real adaptation (near-optimal with only ~50 real samples/category) and robust cross-modal shape completion from partial sketches, which is relevant to real interactive VR design workflows.
Reports generation speed and training cost, supporting reproducibility and practical feasibility claims.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to only four object categories with a relatively small real test set (400 pairs, 100 per category), leaving open how well the approach generalizes to more complex, non-ShapeNet-style, or highly irregular geometries.

The real sketch dataset was collected from only 15 participants; user variability in drawing style, order, and skill is likely underrepresented, and no user study assesses the usability or intuitiveness of the VR sketching interface itself despite this being a stated motivation.

The heuristic synthetic stroke-ordering procedure (DFS traversal with 10% stochastic skipping) is a coarse approximation of genuine human design intent; while shown empirically effective, its fidelity to real cognitive sketching order is not directly validated beyond downstream task performance.

Generation quality is fundamentally bounded by the frozen pretrained 3D VQ-VAE operating at 64^3 resolution, which the authors acknowledge causes oversmoothing and limits fine geometric detail—an inherent limitation not addressed by the proposed contributions.

Comparison to at least one relevant prior method (Chen et al.) could not be performed due to unavailable code/checkpoints, slightly limiting completeness of the baseline comparison, though this is an understandable practical constraint.

Several pipeline hyperparameters (curvature threshold, culling/merging thresholds, stochasticity rate) appear manually tuned without sensitivity analysis, raising minor questions about robustness to different shape categories or sketch styles.

Quantitative evaluation relies solely on Chamfer Distance and F-score; these metrics may not fully capture structural/topological correctness or design-intent preservation that the sequential ordering is meant to encode.

strengths: Introduces a new multi-category (4 categories) VR sketch dataset with both synthetic (20k+) and real (900) sketch-shape pairs, addressing scarcity in a field where prior public benchmarks were single-category (chairs only) and much smaller.

The order-aware sketch encoder is well motivated and empirically validated: ablations (Tab. 4, Tab. A-1) convincingly show that removing stroke/point ordering degrades performance, and that scrambling points is more harmful than scrambling strokes, supporting the paper's central claim.

Strong and fairly comprehensive experimental validation: comparisons against two baselines (Luo et al., LAS-Diffusion) on both an existing benchmark (3DVRChair) and the new dataset, with consistent and large margins of improvement in F-score and Chamfer Distance.

Extensive supplementary analysis covering many practical concerns: partial-sketch/shape-completion, free-hand sketches without reference, unsnapped sketches, unseen categories/datasets (ModelNet), sketcher expertise, and inference speed/precision tradeoffs — this breadth strengthens claims of robustness and generalization.
A user study with 38 participants and 1900 ratings adds human-centered validation beyond automatic metrics, supporting real-world usability claims.
The synthetic sketch generation pipeline is learning-free and clearly described, offering a practical, reproducible way to scale training data without costly human annotation.
Reasonable engineering novelty in adapting BERT-style encoding to 3D ordered stroke/point sequences with Fourier positional features, differentiated clearly from the closest prior work (SketchBERT).
weaknesses: The technical novelty of the model itself is somewhat incremental: it largely combines existing components (BERT-style transformer, Fourier positional encoding, SDFusion diffusion backbone) with relatively modest architectural innovation limited to encoding indices via Fourier features; the core diffusion generator (SDFusion) is unmodified.

The 'order matters' framing is partially undercut by the authors' own ablation (Tab. A-1[C]): reversing stroke order has little effect on performance, suggesting the model may be primarily benefiting from having *some* consistent positional/index information rather than truly learning temporal/design-intent semantics from human drawing order, a nuance under-emphasized in the main paper's narrative.

Evaluation resolution is limited to 64^3 SDF grids (acknowledged as a limitation), which may mask finer geometric differences between methods and limits the practical fidelity of generated shapes compared to state-of-the-art 3D generation methods outside this specific sketch-conditioned niche.

The real dataset, while larger than prior single-category benchmarks, is still modest in scale (900 real sketches, 4 categories) and collected by only 15 participants, raising some questions about diversity of drawing styles despite the free-hand and expertise studies.

Baseline comparison is limited to two direct competitors (Luo et al., LAS-Diffusion); other relevant sketch-to-3D or CAD-sequence methods are discussed in related work but not empirically compared, partly due to lack of released code, which is an understandable but still limiting evaluation gap.

The paper does not provide statistical significance testing for the reported improvements or user study results beyond means and standard deviations, making it harder to assess robustness of the reported gains, especially for smaller-scale comparisons (e.g., few-shot adaptation curves).

Explanation for the counter-intuitive finding that non-expert sketches yield higher reconstruction accuracy than expert sketches (Sec. A-6) is only a post-hoc hypothesis without deeper investigation, leaving an interesting but unresolved result.

strengths: Introduces a new, larger, multi-category (4 categories) dataset with both synthetic (20.8k) and real (900) sequential VR sketches, filling a clear gap given that the only prior public benchmark (3DVRChair) had a single category and 1,005 pairs.

The surface-snapping VR interface for real data collection is a sensible and demonstrably effective solution to the depth-ambiguity problem in VR sketching, quantitatively shown to reduce sketch-to-shape Chamfer distance versus prior datasets.

The learning-free synthetic sketch generation pipeline (salient point extraction, spline fitting, culling, DFS-based stroke ordering) is well described and practically useful for scaling training data without expensive human annotation.

The order-aware BERT-style encoder that jointly encodes 3D point coordinates, stroke index, and point index via Fourier features is a reasonable and clearly motivated architectural contribution, clearly differentiated from SketchBERT.

Strong and fairly comprehensive empirical validation: comparisons on both 3DVRChair and the new dataset, ablations isolating ordering/augmentation/pretraining/encoding choices, a user study on free-hand sketches, partial-sketch/shape-completion experiments, unseen-category generalization, sketch-snapping robustness, sketcher-expertise analysis, and inference-speed/DDIM-step tradeoffs -- this breadth substantially strengthens the claims.

Results show large, consistent margins over baselines (Luo et al., LAS-Diffusion) across nearly all settings and metrics, and the model generalizes well from synthetic-only training to real sketches with little or no fine-tuning, which is a practically valuable property.

The paper is generally clearly written, with an extensive supplementary material section that proactively addresses many natural reviewer questions (unseen classes, snapping ablation, DDIM steps, expertise).
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is somewhat incremental: it largely combines existing components (BERT-style transformer encoder, Fourier positional encodings, SDFusion diffusion backbone) rather than introducing fundamentally new modeling techniques; novelty rests mainly on the sequential-ordering framing and the new dataset/pipeline rather than a substantially new architecture.

The synthetic sketch generation pipeline explicitly does not model human drawing behavior (as stated in the supplementary, 'not intended to model human drawing behavior'), yet the main claim 'order matters' is partly validated using order derived from this heuristic rather than genuine human stroke order; the supplementary ablation on order perturbations (reverse order has 'little effect') somewhat undercuts the strength of the paper's central 'order matters' narrative, and this tension is only partially and briefly reconciled ('reframe our claim...to these empirically supported points') rather than being addressed directly in the main text.

The user study, while informative, is relatively small in scale (38 participants, 40 free-hand/reference sketches, 100 constructed pairs) and does not report statistical significance testing between the two methods' Likert ratings.

Reconstruction quality is bounded by a frozen, pretrained 3D VQ-VAE with 64^3 SDF resolution, which the authors acknowledge limits fine geometric detail (visible oversmoothing); this constrains the method's usefulness for applications needing higher-fidelity outputs, and no experiments explore end-to-end training or higher resolution to address this.

Real dataset scale, while larger than 3DVRChair, is still modest (900 real sketches across 4 categories, ~200-300 per category), and only one participant pool (15 annotators) was used for the main dataset, which may limit stylistic diversity despite the free-hand and unseen-class supplementary experiments.

Some ablations (e.g., 'w/o pretraining' collapsing entirely, matching intuitive expectations) are somewhat expected findings rather than novel insights, and the quantitative gain attributed specifically to 'order' vs. other confounded factors (e.g., extra positional tokens acting as additional capacity) is not fully isolated.
